idiom_name: typed view function returning template literals, or a typed engine render helper
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits template literals and tagged templates, so the page can be typed end to end: declare a locals interface for the page and let the compiler decide which fields the markup may read, which the classic scriptlet has never offered (JSP and Razor report a wrong field name at request time). A tag function can return a branded safe-HTML type so that plain strings cannot reach the response unchecked, and engines such as EJS or Eta can be wrapped in a render helper that takes the same typed locals when a .ejs/.eta artifact is preferred. The native form remains justified for small SSR pages and email rendering; the file-template form when the markup is owned by non-programmers.
pitfalls: Types cover the locals, not the HTML: a renamed field is caught, a missing closing tag or a mis-quoted attribute is not, so a validator or snapshot test still earns its place.
Escaping away from the type system (as any, non-null assertions, an untyped render(template, anything) helper) removes exactly the guarantee that justified choosing TypeScript here.
Template engines keep their locals untyped unless every call site applies the interface, and a branded safe-HTML type must be enforced on the return path or the brand is decorative.
A tagged template only escapes if the tag does it; a tag that concatenates without escaping is a typed alias for string concatenation and gets no help from the compiler.
